questions.stem: What is the scrambled, unreadable format produced by encryption called?
options: Plaintext
CipherText
Hash
Checksum
Token
questions.explanation: Encryption converts normal text into a scrambled format to make it unreadable, which is called CipherText.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of data-at-rest?
options: Data moving from a laptop to a thumb drive
Data shown to a user in a BI dashboard
Data sitting in a database, data warehouse or data lake
Data travelling through the Internet
Data displayed on a web portal such as LinkedIn
questions.explanation: Data-at-rest is data sitting in your database, data warehouse, data lake or in-memory solutions such as Delta Lake, Databricks or Snowflake.

options: Data stored in an in-memory platform
Data moving between devices, within private networks, through the Internet or to a thumb drive
Data exposed to end users in a BI tool
Data that has been decrypted for analysis
Data archived on tape
questions.explanation: Data-in-transit is data moving between devices, such as within private networks, through the Internet, or from laptop to thumb drive, and it must all be encrypted.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of data-in-use?
options: Data in a Snowflake warehouse
Data travelling over a private network
Data exposed to end users in a BI tool or on a website such as Facebook
Data on a backup drive
Data waiting in a message queue
questions.explanation: Data-in-use is data exposed to end users, which can be in a BI tool or on a website or web portal such as Facebook or LinkedIn.

options: It uses two linked keys, one public and one private
It uses one key to both encode and decode the information
It requires no key at all
It is used only for data-in-transit
It is best suited to very large data sets
questions.explanation: Symmetric key encryption uses one key to both encode and decode the information, and is best used for one-to-one sharing and smaller data sets.

questions.stem: In asymmetric (public-key) cryptography, which key is kept private?
options: The encryption key
The decryption key
Both keys
Neither key
The session key
questions.explanation: In asymmetric cryptography the encryption key is public and can be used by anyone to encrypt, while the opposite key is kept private and used to decrypt.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed among the data encryption standards?
options: Triple DES (3DES)
Blowfish
Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC)
Base64
Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
questions.explanation: The listed standards include DES, 3DES, RSA, Blowfish, Twofish, SSL, ECC, AES and end-to-end encryption; Base64 is not among them.

options: Generates a new key for each message
Compresses the CipherText for storage
Brings the data back to its original format using the key generated at encryption
Classifies data into risk groups
Masks sensitive columns before display
questions.explanation: Decryption is the opposite of encryption and returns data to its original format; the key generated during encryption is also used for decryption.

questions.stem: What does encryption key lifecycle management refer to?
options: Rotating passwords for end users every ninety days
Centrally managing keys from the time they are created until they are deactivated and terminated
Distributing public keys through a website
Storing keys inside the encrypted database itself
Choosing between symmetric and asymmetric algorithms
questions.explanation: Key management means centrally managing encryption keys across their whole lifecycle, from creation until deactivation and termination.

questions.stem: Why is SSL decryption technology recommended as part of implementing encryption?
options: Because it replaces the need for key management
Because it makes symmetric keys unnecessary
Because encryption alone is not enough and SSL technology gives insight into sensitive data at points of egress and ingress
Because it speeds up database queries
Because regulators forbid other standards
questions.explanation: Encryption alone is not enough; SSL decryption technology affords insight into sensitive data at points of egress and ingress, where it is vulnerable.
